name: Alpine meadow
notes: Subalpine-alpine herb meadows and grasslands just above treeline: Alps/Pyrenees mat-grass and fescue meadows, Rocky Mountain wildflower meadows, Tibetan/Himalayan Kobresia meadows. Grasses and sedges dominate with showy forbs.

canopy.name: Swiss stone pine

growth.juvenile_note: Seeds are buried in caches by spotted nutcrackers and germinate in the following spring or the one after, often several seedlings together from one forgotten cache. The seedling has a whorl of 8-12 cotyledons, then single primary needles, then bundles of five soft dark needles; young trees are dense, dark, narrow cones that grow only a few cm a year at the treeline.
growth.source: European Atlas of Forest Tree Species / EUFORGEN Pinus cembra (very slow-growing; seed production from about 40-60 years; ages to about 1,000 years; seeds wingless, dispersed and cached by Nucifraga caryocatactes; germination often delayed to the second year)

canopy.source: Alps and Carpathians high forest; 15–25 m. Nutcracker-planted; treeline forest. Kew POWO for the name; standard floras for range. Restored from the pine catalogue; completed from the European Atlas of Forest Tree Species: needles in fives, 5-9 cm; violet cones 5-8 cm ripening in the second autumn and falling unopened; grey-brown fissured bark.

canopy.name: European larch

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal seedling with 5-7 cotyledons and a tuft of soft single needles on a pinkish stem. In its first years it carries needles singly along long shoots; from the third year short spur shoots bear rosettes of 30-40 soft bright-green needles. Young trees are light, open, narrow cones that turn gold and drop every needle in autumn.
growth.source: EUFORGEN / European Atlas of Forest Tree Species Larix decidua (light-demanding pioneer; fast early growth; seed from 10-15 years open-grown, abundant crops every 3-6 years; ages over 1,000 years in the Alps)

canopy.source: Larix decidua Mill. growth.juvenile_note: Tiny two-winged nutlets sprout in early summer on moss, bare soil or burnt ground. Seedlings have minute round cotyledons, then small, downy, coarsely toothed, rounded leaves on hairy reddish twigs. At the treeline the young tree soon sprouts extra stems from its base, becoming a crooked, multi-stemmed bush with dark reddish-brown bark that whitens and peels only on older stems.
growth.source: Wikipedia (short-lived tree; subarctic mountain birch small, contorted and shrubby); Atkinson 1992 Biological Flora of Betula pendula and B. pubescens (light-demanding pioneer, seed from young age, winged nutlets shed late summer to winter); treeline growth rates and ages estimated.

fruiting.source: General Betula pubescens silvics (Atkinson 1992): catkins open with the leaves in spring (May-Jun in the subarctic), wind-pollinated, fruiting catkins 2-3.5 cm break up on the tree from late summer through winter; counts are catkins, estimated.

shrub.name: Alpenrose

growth.juvenile_note: Minute seedlings on moss or raw humus: two tiny cotyledons, then small glossy, dark green, leathery leaves with rusty-brown scaly undersides and rolled edges. For years it is a small, few-stemmed sprig; then it branches densely into a low, rounded evergreen bush, and stems that touch the ground root and spread it into a clonal patch.
growth.source: German Wikipedia Rostblaettrige Alpenrose (30-130 cm; stems 1-2 cm thick nearly 100 yr old; leaves live ~2 yr; flowers May-Jul, corolla to 2 cm, deep pink to red; capsules to 7 mm ripen from August; semi-shade light value; 440-2,840 m); germination and first flowering estimated

shrub.source: Alps subalpine; Heath above the trees. Kew POWO; standard floras.

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: two tiny round cotyledons, then small oblong leaves with rounded teeth, glossy dark green above and white-woolly beneath, like miniature oak leaves. The seedling's woody stem creeps and branches over limestone gravel, rooting as it goes, and slowly builds a flat evergreen mat that carries eight-petalled white flowers and twisting feathery seed plumes.
growth.source: Wikipedia Dryas octopetala (creamy white flowers with 8, occasionally up to 16, petals on 3-10 cm stalks; persistent feathery styles twisted, then spreading into a ball for wind dispersal; early-melting gravel and rock barrens, mostly on limestone). Mat growth, first flowering and age estimated (Elkington 1971 Biol. Flora, not read).

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: 2 (up to 6) slender cotyledons, then whorls of three sharp, needle-like leaves with a white band above - the same prickly needles the adult keeps all its life (it never makes scale leaves). Seedlings are tiny, slow, prickly sprigs that build over decades into a dense, spreading grey-green shrub, a low mat, or a narrow column.
growth.source: USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual (Juniperus: J. communis flowers Apr-May, cones take 2-3 seasons, green to bluish-black glaucous, persist; 1-3 seeds; bears from 10-20 yr, heavy crops every 2-5 yr; deep dormancy; 2-6 cotyledons); Wikipedia (ripens in 18 months, cones 4-12 mm, a Lapland plant aged 1,647 yr). Growth rate estimated.

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (dioecious, wind-pollinated; berry-like cones 4-12 mm, green ripening in ~18 months to purple-black with a blue bloom; too bitter raw, dried as spice and for gin); USDA WPSM (2-3 seasons to ripen, cones persist). Set, crop and rot estimated.

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling minute: 2 round cotyledons and a pair of small, round, glossy leaves on a thread stem. Its woody stems creep just UNDER the soil and send up shoots only 1-6 cm tall, each with 2-3 round, finely toothed, shiny leaves and one tiny catkin; over decades it spreads as an open carpet in snowbeds. Genets in the Apennines are at least 2,000 years old.
growth.source: Wikipedia/Flora of GB Salix herbacea (1-6 cm tall, stems creep underground forming open mats; genets in the N Apennines at least 2,000 yr old; female catkins red when ripe); USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual Salix (fast germination); spread rate and first seed estimated

growth.juvenile_note: A seedling tuft of stiff, bristle-like, grey-green leaves. It slowly grows into a dense, tough, wiry tussock whose leaves stick out at wide angles like a bottle brush over a base packed with persistent pale sheaths; slim one-sided purplish flower spikes stand on thin stems in early summer. Grazers avoid it, so it thickens on heavily grazed acid grassland.
growth.source: Chadwick 1960, Biological Flora of the British Isles: Nardus stricta (J. Ecol. 48) for habit, slow seedling growth and grazing avoidance; ages and rates estimated
